etymologies.etymologyHTML: From late Middle English mature, from Middle French mature, from Latin mātūrus. Doublet of maduro. Partially displaced ripe, from Old English rīpe (“ripe, mature”).

definitions.definition: Fully developed; grown up in terms of physical appearance, behaviour or thinking; ripe.
Brought to a state of complete readiness.
(medicine, obsolete) Come to, or in a state of, completed suppuration.
(television, film) Suitable for adults only, due to sexual themes, violence, etc.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English maturen, from Middle French maturer (“to mature”), from Latin mātūrō.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To proceed toward maturity: full development or completion (either of concrete or of abstract things, e.g. plans, judgments, qualities).

quote.citation: 1797, Mr. Harrison, “A Biographical Sketch of Hogarth”, in The Comick Magazine‎[1], volume 1, London: Harrison and Co., page 3:
quote.text: […]  his originality, in the mean time, was maturing to perfection.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, of food, especially fruit) To attain maturity, to become mature or ripe.

quote.citation: 1670, John Evelyn, chapter 35, in Sylva, or, A Discourse of Forest-trees‎[2], London, page 246:
quote.text: […]  Trees  […]  have alwayes Fruit upon them, ripe, or preparing to mature;

definitions.definition: (transitive) To bring (something) to maturity, full development, or completion.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, Paradise Lost‎[3], book 1, lines 659–660:
quote.text: […]  But these thoughtsFull Counsel must mature:

quote.citation: 1768, John Hoole, Cyrus: A Tragedy‎[4], London: T. Davies, act I, page 12:
quote.text: […]  much it nowImports they should be still deceiv’d, till timeMatures our enterprize;

quote.citation: 1853, Elizabeth Gaskell, Cranford, New York: Harper, Chapter 13, p. 262,[5]:
quote.text: […]  I did not interrupt her, I was so busy maturing a plan I had had in my mind for some days  […]

quote.citation: 1953, Saul Bellow, chapter 8, in The Adventures of Augie March, New York: Viking Press, →OCLC, page 143:
quote.text: […]  the long clean groove of her upper lip was ready to go into motion, as if she were going to break her silence with something momentous and long-matured; explain love to me, perhaps.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make (something, e.g. fruit) ripe or mature.

quote.citation: 1782, William Cowper, “Charity”, in Poems‎[6], London: J. Johnson, page 202:
quote.text: […]  a ship well freighted with the storesThe sun matures on India’s spicy shores,

quote.citation: 2009, Hugh Findlay, Practical Gardening, Vegetables and Fruits‎[7]:
quote.text: There are certain vegetables like the tomato which require a long period to mature the fruit, and these must be started several weeks before the frosts have passed.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, of a person) To proceed toward or become mature or full-grown, either physically or psychologically; to gain experience or wisdom with age.

quote.citation: 1776, Hannah Cowley, The Runaway‎[8], London: Prologue:
quote.text: Then Tom shall have his kite, and Fan new dollies,Till time matures them for important follies.

quote.citation: 1970, Robertson Davies, chapter 2, in Fifth Business‎[9], part 6, Toronto: Macmillan, page 103:
quote.text: […]  what I most wanted was time to grow up. The war had not matured me;

definitions.definition: (intransitive, finance) To reach the date when payment is due.
